                       Γ.BPPV
                           .Key questions to ask during the patient interview (!!E)
                              Γ(See also: [NM1 06.mp4] 44:36sec)
                              • Do you get dizzy (spin) when you roll over in bed?
                              • Do you get dizzy (spin) when you sit up in the morning or lie down at night?
                              • Do you get dizzy (spin) when you look up or bend over?
                              • Can you lie flat without a pillow?
                              • How long do your symptoms last?
                                 • Response should be seconds to a minute (not all patients can reliably tell you this though)
                           .Provoking Positions
                              • Getting out of bed
                              • Lying down from sit to supine
                              • Bending over
                              • Looking up or reaching overhead
                              • Rolling in bed
                              • Going from supine to sit
                              • An inability to sleep without several pillows
                           .Other provoking positions
                              Washing hair
                              Dental chairs
                              Painting overhead
                              Changing a light bulb
                              Working under the car/plumbing
                              Getting clothes out of the dryer

                       (Γ)Step 2 of the Framework
                               2.a. History, Observation, and Review of Systems
                               2.b. Sensory Exam  
                                  - Light Touch screen  
                                  - S/D  
                                  - Proprioception  
                               3.c. Balance Exam  
                                  - Standing (and Sitting) Balance:  
                                    - Static Standing Balance: Sensory orientation and reactive postural control  
                                    - Dynamic Standing Balance: Self-generated voluntary postural control  
                                    - Walking Balance  
                               4.d. Mental Status Exam  
                                  - Basic Mental Functions, Complex Mental Functions, and Meta-cognitive Functions  
                               5.e. Motor Exam  
                                  - Muscle Mass  
                                  - ROM  
                                  - Tone  
                                  - Muscle Capacity (Strength [force production], Endurance, Power)  
                                  - Motor Control of Movement/Stability  
                                  - Observation of Involuntary Movements

                                  - Changing and Maintaining Body Positions:  
                                    - Bed mobility  
                                    - Sit <-> Stand  
                                    - Transfers  
                                  - Mobility:  
                                    - Walking (level surface and complex situations)  
                                    - Stairs

                                    - Grasping & Object Manipulation

                   Γxº.PT Diagnosis?
                       (Γ).What Happens When There is Vestibular System Dysfunction?
                           Γ.Dizziness
                              .The PT differential diagnosis is critical
                                 • Testing must be done to determine what exactly is the patient's problem
                                 • Often patients present to the clinic with a diagnosis of “dizziness” which is not enough information for any clinician to design an appropriate treatment plan
                                    Identification of red flags/yellow flags
                                       .Central Signs and Symptoms – Red Flags
                                           • Cranial nerve signs
                                               • Changes in pupillary size
                                               • Ptosis
                                               • Difficulty with swallowing
                                           • Other neurologic signs
                                               • Downbeat nystagmus
                                               • Cerebellar signs and symptoms
                                               • Headaches
                                                   .Vestibular Migraine
                                               • Associated head injuries/cervical dysfunction
                                               • A sense of tilting by the patient
                                               • Changes in sensation
                                               • A positive Babinski, increased DTR’s, or clonus
                                               • Impaired gait/ataxia
                                          ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                          .Assessment for CNS signs
                                             • Cranial nerve exam
                                                 • Pupil size and symmetry
                                                 • Ocular ROM, alignment
                                                 • Conjugate gaze (smooth pursuits and saccades)
                                                 • Facial symmetry
                                                 • Hearing
                                                 • Dysarthria
                                                 • Dysphagia
                                             • Sensory exam
                                             • Motor exam
                                                 • UMN signs
                                             • Coordination exam
                                                 • Dysdiadokokinesia
                                                 • Dysmetria
                                                 • Ataxia
                                    Differences in management
                                    Differences in prognosis
                                 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                 .Screening for psychosocial factors
                                    • Anxiety: GAD-7
                                    • Depression: PHQ-9
                                    • Anxiety & Depression quick screen: PHQ-4
                                    • Fear Avoidance: 
                                       • Vestibular Activities Avoidance Instrument
                                       • Fear Avoidance Behavior after Traumatic Brain Injury Questionnaire
                                    • Catastrophizing: Dizziness Catastrophizing Scale
                                    • www.phqscreeners.com 
                              .Not all dizziness is caused by vestibular disorders
                                 List of potential causes
                                     - Medications  
                                     - Postural hypotension  
                                     - Diabetes  
                                     - Thyroid conditions  
                                     - Renal failure  
                                     - Psychiatric illness
                                 Pie chart: Distribution of causes of dizziness 
                                     - Cardiovascular disease (including CVA) 58%  
                                     - Peripheral vestibular disease 14%  
                                     - Psychiatric illness 10%  
                                     - Unclear 8%  
                                     - Locomotor disease 4%  
                                     - Neurologic disease (not CVA) 3%  
                                     - Drug side effect 2%  
                                     - Metabolic/endocrine 1%
                                 Concluding statement 
                                     - Dizziness is NEVER normal – no matter what your age!
                                 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                 ✗.Drug-Associated Dizziness (!!E)
                                    • Aminoglycosides can cause vertigo and disequilibrium (they also 
                                    damage the vestibular hair cells)
                                    • Antiepileptics can cause disequilibrium (also cerebellar toxicity and 
                                    CNS depression)
                                    • Tranquilizers can cause dizziness and CNS depression
                                    • Anti-hypertensives can cause postural hypotension and decreased 
                                    CNS blood flow
                                    • Alcohol can cause disequilibrium resulting in CNS depression, 
                                    damage to the cerebellum, and changes in the specific gravity of the 
                                    cupula
                           .What to do if you suspect a vestibular disorder?
                               • Treat the patient
                               • Refer the patient to another therapist who has greater expertise
                               • Refer back to the physician (non urgent)
                               • Refer to a physician (non-urgent) AND treat the patient
                               • Refer to a physician or ED (urgent)
                               • Might refer the patient for adjunct treatment AND treat the patient
                                 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                 .Urgent referrals back to the physician
                                    • Loss of consciousness
                                    • Changes in mental status, significant cognitive changes
                                    • Repeated, unexplained serious falls
                                    • Patient reports a sensation of being pushed off balance
                                    • Having the worst headache of their life
                                    • Cranial nerve signs
                                        • Visual field loss
                                        • Changes in pupillary size or ptosis
                                        • Facial asymmetry
                                        • Sudden hearing loss
                                        • Swallowing difficulties
                                    • UMN signs and symptoms
                                        • Increased DTRs
                                        • Positive Babinski
                                        • Clonus
                                    • Changes in sensation that are not explained by premorbid impairments
                                 .Non-urgent referral back to the physician (!!E).Lv1
                                     • Signs and symptoms not consistent with vestibular disorder
                                     • Findings with psychological screenings
                                     • Ocular misalignment or visual changes impacting ADLs (either pre-existing or co-existing with vestibular disorder)
                                     • Hearing loss (gradual)
                                     • The patient has not gotten better or has gotten worse after treating the patient for 3-5 visits
                                 .TiTrATE: Timing, Triggers, and Targeted Exam
                                    See graph ('')
                           ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                           • Peripheral
                              (1)------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                  • Acute unilateral vestibulopathy  
                                  • Bilateral vestibulopathy  
                                  • Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
                              (2)------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                  Peripheral Vestibular Disorder
                                    A lesion affecting the semicircular canals, otolith organs, or vestibulocochlear nerve
                              (3)------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                  .Central vs. Peripheral nystagmus (!!E).Lv1.Q&A doc
                                      • Peripheral
                                          • Direction fixed
                                          • Intensity decreases with visual fixation
                                          • Follows Alexander’s law
                                          • May be persistent or brief (BPPV)
                              (4)------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                  .Nystagmus
                                     1. Peripheral Vestibular Disorders:
                                       - Peripheral Spontaneous Nystagmus: Horizontal nystagmus, often associated with BPPV or vestibular neuritis.
                                       - Symmetric Gaze-Evoked Nystagmus: Horizontal nystagmus provoked by extreme gaze positions, also linked to peripheral vestibular issues.
                              (5)------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                  .Vestibular-specific tests: Central vs. Peripheral (!!E).Lv1
                                      • VOR assessment
                                          • Findings that indicate a peripheral disorder
                                              • Positive HIT (unilateral or bilateral)
                                              • Horizontal nystagmus post-head shake
                                              • Horizontal nystagmus with vibration to the mastoid
                                              • Normal VOR cancellation
                              (6)------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                  .Positioning Tests: Differentiating between Peripheral and Central Paroxysmal Positional Nystagmus
                                      Table: Comparison by Category
                                      - Appearance  
                                        - Peripheral (BPPV): Torsional upbeat or horizontal  
                                        - Central: Pure vertical, usually downbeat

                                      - Latency  
                                        - Peripheral (BPPV): Usual  
                                        - Central: Unusual

                                      - Fatigability  
                                        - Peripheral (BPPV): Usual  
                                        - Central: Unusual

                                      - Mechanism  
                                        - Peripheral (BPPV): Debris moving in the semicircular canal  
                                        - Central: Damage to the central vestibulo-ocular pathways

                                      - Localization  
                                        - Peripheral (BPPV): Posterior or horizontal semicircular canal  
                                        - Central: Brain stem or cerebellum
                              (7)------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                 .Peripheral Vestibular Disorders
                                    ✓• Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo
                                       .What is BPPV?
                                           • It is a mechanical problem within the peripheral 
                                           vestibular system
                                           • Otoconia are displaced from the otolith organs into one 
                                           of the semicircular canals
                                           • When the head is moved relative to gravity, the 
                                           otoconia move in the canal and cause the endolymph to 
                                           move, deflecting the cupula
                                           • This causes excitation to the vestibular nuclei resulting 
                                           in dizziness, nausea, and vomiting (often associated 
                                           with position change)
                                           • Caused by free floating otoconia – called canalithiasis
                                           • Otoconia can also get “stuck” in the canal (likely at the 
                                           cupula) and is called cupulolithiasis
                                       .What causes BPPV?
                                           • Idiopathic
                                           • Traumatic event
                                       .What factors are associated with BPPV?
                                           • Ageing
                                           • Associated with peripheral vestibular dysfunction 
                                               • Meniere's disease 
                                               • Peripheral vestibular hypofunction
                                           • TBI 
                                               • Estimates up to 58% with BPPV
                                           • Migraines
                                           • Osteoporosis
                                           • Post-surgical? (positioning in OR)
                                       .BPPV Related to Osteoporosis and Vitamin D
                                       .Seasonality of Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo ('')
                                    ✓• Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy
                                       .Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy (AUVP) ('')
                                          • Synonymous with vestibular neuritis
                                          • Pathophysiology
                                              • Inflammation of the vestibular nerve
                                          • Likely etiology
                                              • Viral
                                              • Autoimmune
                                              • Vascular
                                          ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                             .Diagnostic Criteria for AUVP
                                                 • Acute or subacute onset or sustained spinning or non-spinning vertigo of moderate to severe intensity lasting at least 24 hours
                                                 • Spontaneous peripheral vestibular nystagmus
                                                     • Generally horizontal-torsional
                                                     • Direction-fixed (unidirectional)
                                                     • Enhanced by removal of visual fixation
                                                 • Unambiguous evidence of reduced VOR function on the side opposite the direction of the fast phase of the nystagmus
                                                     • HIT (preferred vHIT), caloric test
                                                 • No evidence of acute central neurological or audiological symptoms 
                                                 • No acute central neurological or audiological signs (skew deviation, gaze-evoked nystagmus)
                                                 • Not better accounted for by another disease process or disorder
                                          ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                             .AUVP: Typical Symptom Report
                                                • Dizziness
                                                    • Spinning (vertigo), oscillopsia
                                                    • Initially constant then decreasing in severity/frequency
                                                    • May be worse with head motion/position changes
                                                • Poor balance but usually can ambulate
                                                • Nausea/vomiting initially
                                                • Onset may be associated with an upper respiratory/viral illness
                                             .AUVP: Atypical Symptom Report
                                                • Hearing loss, tinnitus, fullness may indicate other peripheral or central disorders
                                                • Headache (more frequently seen in persons with central disorders)
                                                • Inability to walk/ataxic gait
                                                • Diplopia (double vision)
                                                • Lightheadedness
                                          ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                             .AUVP: Typical Signs
                                                 • Acutely, spontaneous nystagmus will be seen in room light
                                                     • Direction-fixed (unidirectional)
                                                     • More intense without visual fixation
                                                     • Typically, horizontal-torsional
                                                 • Within days, the static VOR should compensate
                                                 • After static compensation of the VOR, may still see nystagmus but not as severe as that seen acute phase
                                                     • May only see with fixation blocked
                                                     • May only see first or second-degree nystagmus compared to third degree
                                          ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                             .AUVP: Medical Management
                                                 Medication Management
                                                     • Treatment with methylprednisolone tapering dose schedule
                                                         • Research is mixed regarding the effectiveness of steroid management for long-term outcomes
                                                     • Medications for symptom management
                                                         • Antiemetics for nausea
                                                         • Anticholinergics, antihistamines
                                                 Tests and Measures
                                                     • Vestibular function testing
                                                         • Caloric test
                                                         • Rotational chair
                                                         • VEMPs
                                                         • vHIT
                                                     • May have had MRI to rule out central diagnoses
                                                 Early Vestibular Rehabilitation = better outcomes for AUVP!
                                          ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                             .What PT Tests and Measures Should be Used?
                                                 • Screen for central neurologic signs and auditory symptoms
                                                     • Hearing screen
                                                     • HINTS
                                                     • Neurologic exam (cranial nerve, UMN, cerebellar signs)
                                                 • Oculomotor assessment
                                                 • VOR assessment
                                                 • Positional testing (BPPV present in 15-20% of individuals with peripheral vestibular disorders)
                                                 • Balance, gait, functional exam
                                          ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                             .AUVP: PT Exam Findings
                                                 • No central vestibular or neurologic signs
                                                     • No UMN, cerebellar signs
                                                     • Normal oculomotor exam
                                                 • No hearing loss
                                                 • Positional testing
                                                     • May or may not have co-occurring BPPV
                                                 • VOR assessments
                                                     • Positive HIT
                                                     • Positive head shake test
                                                     • Positive DVA
                                                     • Positive vibration-induced nystagmus
                                                 • Balance, gait, functional exam
                                                     • Difficulty standing on foam with eyes closed (condition 4 mCTSIB)
                                                     • Difficulty walking with head turns
                                                     • Difficulty with turns, quick head movements, position changes
                                          ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                             .When to Refer Out
                                                 • They have new headaches with the onset of the vertigo
                                                 • If you note neurologic signs and symptoms
                                                 • If the vertigo has not improved at all within 48 hours
                                                 • New onset hearing loss with the onset of vertigo
                                                 • HINTS exam positive
                                    ✓• Chronic Unilateral Vestibulopathy
                                       .Chronic Unilateral Vestibulopathy
                                           • Typically refers to those who have had symptoms for > 3 months
                                           • Dynamic VOR may be uncompensated or only partially compensated
                                           • Potential factors that may impact recovery:
                                               • Comorbidities
                                                   • Number of comorbid conditions
                                                   • Binocular vision abnormalities
                                                   • Cognitive impairment
                                                   • Anxiety
                                                   • Depression
                                                   • CNS diagnoses
                                               • Long-term vestibular suppressant medication use
                                               • Avoidance of movement, activity
                                           • Individuals with Chronic Unilateral Vestibulopathy still benefit from vestibular rehabilitation
                                       .Chronic Unilateral Vestibulopathy Findings
                                           • Spontaneous nystagmus should not be present
                                           • May see nystagmus with fixation blocked, although may only be first degree
                                           • VOR assessments
                                               • Clinical HIT may or may not be positive
                                               • vHIT would likely be positive
                                               • Head shake, DVA, vibration-induced nystagmus may or may not be positive
                                           • Balance, gait, and functional assessments
                                               • Likely difficulty on condition 4 of mCTSIB
                                               • Difficulty with higher level gait involving head turns, turning, etc.
                                    ✓• Bilateral Vestibulopathy
                                       .Bilateral Vestibulopathy
                                           • Bilateral impairment or loss of peripheral vestibular input
                                           • Results in deficits such as:
                                               • Impaired VOR
                                               • Impaired VSR
                                               • Difficulty with spatial orientation, navigation, and memory
                                           • Likely etiology
                                               • Result of ototoxic drugs (antibiotics, chemotherapy, loop diuretics)
                                               • Bilateral Meniere’s disease
                                               • Meningitis/Inflammation
                                               • Tumors
                                               • Autoimmune disease
                                               • Genetic factors
                                       .Bilateral Vestibulopathy: Diagnostic Criteria
                                          • Chronic vestibular syndrome with unsteadiness when walking or standing and at least 1 of the following:
                                              • Movement-induced blurred vision or oscillopsia during walking or quick body movements
                                              • Worsening of unsteadiness in darkness or on uneven ground
                                          • No symptoms when sitting or lying down (static conditions)
                                          • Bilaterally reduced or absent angular VOR 
                                              • vHIT
                                              • Caloric response
                                              • Rotational chair
                                          • Not better accounted for by another disease 
                                       .Bilateral Vestibulopathy: Typical Signs and Symptoms
                                          • Oscillopsia: visual jumping of the environment with movement
                                          • Postural instability
                                          • Gait impairments (wide based)
                                          • History of falls
                                          • Vertigo not usually described
                                       .Bilateral Vestibulopathy: PT Exam Findings
                                          • VOR assessment
                                              • HIT: positive bilaterally
                                              • DVA: usually significant loss of visual acuity with head movement (>2 lines)
                                          • Balance assessment
                                              • Loss of balance eyes closed
                                              • Difficulty with conditions 2, 4, and sometimes 3 of mCTSIB
                                          • Gait assessment
                                              • Gait deviations (wide based gait, gait may appear ataxic)
                                              • Difficulty on uneven surfaces, low light conditions
                                          • Should guard the patient closely when assessing balance and gait!
                                    • Other peripheral vestibular disorders
                                       ✓• Labyrinthitis
                                          .Labyrinthitis
                                             Γ No confundir amb "Labyrinthine infarct" de la secció "• Central"
                                             • Inflammation of the entire labyrinth (blue in figure)
                                             • Symptoms are similar to AUVP
                                             • Typically, also experience:
                                                 • Hearing loss
                                                 • Ear pain
                                                 • Tinnitus (ringing)
                                             • Management similar to AUVP
                                             • Important to refer out if you find hearing loss and/or ear symptoms
                                          .Pattern of Symptoms
                                             1. Reduced Vestibular Function
                                                - Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy
                                                  - Tempo: Sudden onset; acute dizziness
                                                  - Symptoms: Vertigo, imbalance, N/V, oscillopsia
                                                  - Circumstance: Spontaneous, exacerbated by head movement
                                                - Labyrinthitis
                                                  - Tempo: Sudden onset; acute dizziness
                                                  - Symptoms: As above; hearing loss; tinnitus
                                                  - Circumstance: Spontaneous, exacerbated by head movement
                                                - Chronic Unilateral Vestibulopathy
                                                  - Tempo: Chronic dizziness
                                                  - Symptoms: Dizziness, imbalance
                                                  - Circumstance: Induced by head movement; complex environment
                                                - Bilateral Vestibulopathy
                                                  - Tempo: Post-treatment with ototoxic medications
                                                  - Symptoms: Imbalance, oscillopsia
                                                  - Circumstance: Imbalance and/or oscillopsia with movement
                                       ✓• Meniere’s Disease
                                          .Meniere’s Disease
                                             • Synonymous with endolymphatic hydrops
                                             • Accumulation of endolymph in the cochlear duct and the vestibular organs
                                             • Etiology: likely combination of genetic and environmental factors
                                             • Prevalence increases with age
                                             • Associated with comorbid conditions such as:
                                                 • Arthritis
                                                 • Psoriasis
                                                 • Gastroesophageal reflux disease
                                                 • Irritable bowel syndrome
                                                 • Migraine
                                             .Meniere’s Disease Diagnostic Criteria
                                                • Two or more spontaneous episodes of vertigo lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours
                                                • Audiometric findings: low to medium frequency sensorineural hearing loss in one ear during or after one of the vertigo episodes
                                                • Fluctuation aural symptoms
                                                    • Hearing
                                                    • Tinnitus
                                                    • Fullness
                                                • Not better accounted for by another vestibular diagnosis
                                          .Meniere’s Disease Typical Signs and Symptoms
                                              • Acute dizziness/vertigo lasting hours
                                              • Nausea/vomiting
                                              • Aural symptoms: hearing loss, tinnitus, fullness on the affected side
                                              • Drop attacks
                                          .Meniere's Disease: Medical Management
                                              • Dietary recommendations: limit sodium and caffeine
                                              • Vestibular rehabilitation between attacks
                                              • Pharmacological management
                                                  • Diuretic medication
                                                  • Vasodilators, immunotherapy?
                                                  • Intratympanic steroids
                                              • Vestibular ablation
                                                  • Intratympanic gentamycin
                                                  • Surgical
                                                  • Vestibular neurectomy
                                                  • Labyrinthectomy
                                              • Endolymphatic sac surgery
                                       ✓• Ramsay Hunt Syndrome
                                          .Ramsay Hunt Syndrome
                                              • Herpes zoster (shingles) infection of CN VII/VIII
                                              • Clinical presentation:
                                                  • Initially burning ear pain and blisters, vertigo, hearing disorders and facial paresis
                                                  • The symptoms can begin before the skin rash or even without a skin rash
                                              • Treatment
                                                  • Corticosteroids
                                                  • Antiviral therapy
                                                  • Pain management
                                                  • Vestibular rehabilitation for vertigo and balance issues
                                                  • Facial nerve therapy
                                       ✓• Superior Canal Dehiscence
                                          .Superior Canal Dehiscence 
                                              • Sound and/or pressure-induced vertigo due to bone dehiscence of the superior semicircular canal
                                              • Abnormality identified on CT temporal bones as dehiscence of the SCC
                                              • Signs and symptoms
                                                  • Loud sounds caused objects in visual surround to move
                                                  • Dizziness induced by sneezing, laughing, coughing, heavy lifting (Valsalva)
                                                  • Conductive hearing loss (low frequency)
                                                  • Hear their voice, heartbeat or even their eyes movements in the affected ear
                                                  • Tulio phenomenon: Recorded eye movements in response to sounds 
                                                  • Hennebert sign: eye movements induced by pressure in the external auditory canal
                                          Γ.Tulio’s Phenomenon ('')
                                          .Superior Semicircular Canal Dehiscence: Treatment
                                             • Conservative management
                                                 • Ear plugs
                                                 • Minimize Valsalva, scuba diving, popping ears
                                             • Surgical
                                                 • For those with debilitating auditory or vestibular symptoms and positive clinical findings and CT findings
                                             • Vestibular rehab may be helpful pre and/or post surgery
                                       • Acoustic neuroma/vestibular schwannoma (may be mixed central/peripheral)
                                          .Cochlear Implants & Vestibular Implants
                                             Cochlear implants
                                                • For profound hearing loss
                                                • Children with cochlear implants may have poorer balance compared to children of similar age without cochlear implant
                                             Vestibular implants
                                                • Ongoing research
                                                • For those with profound bilateral vestibular loss
                           • Central
                              (1)------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                  • Cardiovascular accident (PICA or AICA)  
                                  • Traumatic brain injury  
                                  • Cerebellar disorders  
                                  • Multiple sclerosis
                              (2)------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                  Central Vestibular Disorder
                                     • A lesion affecting any central vestibular structures or pathways
                                         • Areas of the brainstem
                                         • Areas of the cerebellum
                                         • Areas of the cerebral cortex
                                         • Ascending/Descending pathways
                              (3)------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                  .Central vs. Peripheral nystagmus (!!E).Lv1.Q&A doc
                                      • Central
                                          • Vertical nystagmus without torsion
                                          • Intensity stays the same or increases with visual fixation
                                          • Direction-changing not associated with position change
                                          • Persistent (usually)
                              (4)------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                  .Nystagmus
                                    2. Red Flags:
                                       - Congenital Spontaneous Nystagmus: Horizontal nystagmus that is not longstanding (developed later in life) is a red flag for central vestibular or CNS disorders.
                                       - Downbeat Spontaneous Nystagmus: Vertical nystagmus (downward) is always a red flag, indicating potential central vestibular or CNS pathology.
                                          .Vertical Nystagmus in Central Disorders
                                              Spontaneous nystagmus in central vestibular disorder is commonly due to cerebellar disorders
                                              Downbeat nystagmus is the most common type of nystagmus in patients with central disorders in conditions such as:
                                                  Chiari malformation
                                                  Bilateral brainstem lesions
                                                  Bilateral floccular lesions, or lesions of the vestibulocerebellum
                              (5)------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                  .Vestibular-specific tests: Central vs. Peripheral
                                      • VOR assessment
                                          • Findings that indicate a central disorder
                                              • Normal HIT (in the presence of acute dizziness/spontaneous nystagmus)
                                              • Vertical nystagmus post-head shake
                                              • Abnormal VOR cancellation
                              (6)------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                 See the (6) above
                              (7)------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                 .Central Causes of Dizziness
                                     • Degenerative conditions
                                         • Cerebellar degeneration
                                         ✓• Multiple sclerosis
                                              • Focal neurologic signs
                                                  • Oculomotor impairments
                                                  • UMN signs
                                                  • Ataxia, gait disturbances
                                              • Recurrent spontaneous attacks of vertigo (due to lesions in brainstem, cerebellum, vestibular and/or visual pathways)
                                              • Vertical nystagmus that is non fatiguing
                                              • If person is 20-40 years old with the above symptoms, suspect MS
                                     • Acquired conditions
                                         ✓• Traumatic brain injury (concussion reviewed in another module)
                                             .Post-Traumatic Dizziness
                                                • Temporal bone fracture
                                                • Concussion (mTBI)
                                                • Moderate to severe TBI
                                                • Whiplash injuries
                                                    • Cervical vertigo
                                         ✓• CVA, TIA
                                             (Γ)Vascular Vertigo
                                                Mini Índex
                                                   PICA infarct
                                                   AICA infarct
                                                   Labyrinthine infarct
                                                ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                                    Etiology
                                                        • Stroke or transient ischemic attack
                                                            • PICA
                                                               .PICA infarct (Haines atlas)
                                                                   • Results in damage to the dorsolateral medulla (PICA syndrome, Wallenberg syndrome, lateral medullary syndrome) 
                                                                   • In some cases, the lateral medullary syndrome may result from occlusion of the vertebral artery at the origin of the PICA with consequent loss of flow into PICA
                                                                   • Structural Damage
                                                                       • Anterolateral system fibers
                                                                       • Spinal trigeminal tract and nucleus
                                                                       • Nucleus ambiguus, roots of 9th and 10th nerves
                                                                       • Descending hypothalamospinal fibers
                                                                       • Vestibular nuclei (mainly inferior and medial)
                                                                       • Restiform body and spinocerebellar fibers
                                                                   • Deficits:
                                                                       • Contralateral loss of pain and thermal sense on body
                                                                       • Ipsilateral loss of pain and thermal sense on face and in the oral cavity
                                                                       • Dysphagia, soft palate paralysis, hoarseness, diminished gag reflex
                                                                       • Ipsilateral Horner syndrome (miosis, ptosis, anhidrosis, flushing of face)
                                                                       • Nausea, diplopia, tendency to fall to ipsilateral side, nystagmus, vertigo
                                                                       • Ataxia to the ipsilateral side
                                                            • AICA
                                                               .AICA infarct
                                                                   • Supplies the middle cerebellar peduncle, lower lateral pons, anteroinferior surface of the cerebellum, flocculus and the choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle.
                                                                   • The labyrinthine artery (branch of AICA) supplies labyrinth and cochlea of the inner ear along with CN VII and CN VIII
                                                                   • Signs and symptoms:
                                                                       • sudden onset of severe vertigo, nausea, vomiting, nystagmus (vestibular nuclei)
                                                                       • ipsilateral hemiataxia (middle cerebellar peduncle)
                                                                       • ipsilateral, lower motor neuron facial weakness, ipsilateral loss of lacrimation and salivation, ipsilateral loss of taste from anterior 2/3rd of tongue and loss of corneal reflex (CN VII nucleus and nerve)
                                                                       • ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature from the face (spinal trigeminal nucleus) 
                                                                       • ipsilateral hearing loss and tinnitus (cochlear nuclei)
                                                                       • ipsilateral Horner's syndrome (descending sympathetic tracts)
                                                                       • contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation from the body (lateral spinothalamic tract). 
                                                            • Labyrinthine infarct
                                                        • Vertebral artery insufficiency/compression
                                                    Presentation
                                                        • Can present similar to AUVP (acute vestibular syndrome)
                                                            • Dizziness
                                                            • Nausea or vomiting
                                                            • Head motion intolerance
                                                            • Unsteadiness 
                                                        • Can be prolonged (symptoms lasting 24 hours or more) or transient (lasting <24 hours)
                                                   ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                                      .Vascular Vertigo Diagnostic Criteria
                                                          Acute prolonged vascular vertigo 
                                                              • Acute vertigo, dizziness, or unsteadiness lasting for 24 hours or more
                                                              • Imaging evidence of ischemia or hemorrhage in the brain or inner ear, which corresponds to signs, symptoms, and findings
                                                              • Not better accounted for by another disease or disorder
                                                          Transient vascular vertigo or acute vascular vertigo in evolution
                                                              • Acute vertigo, dizziness, or unsteadiness lasting < 24 hours
                                                              • Imaging evidence of ischemia or hemorrhage in the brain or inner ear, which corresponds to signs, symptoms, and findings
                                                              • Not better accounted for by another disease or disorder
                                                      .Probable Vascular Vertigo Diagnostic Criteria
                                                         Prolonged
                                                             • Acute vertigo, dizziness, or unsteadiness lasting for 24 hours or more
                                                             • At least one of the following:
                                                                 • Focal central neurologic signs and symptoms (hemiparesis, sensory loss, dysarthria, dysphagia, ataxia)
                                                                 • At least one component of the HINTS exam
                                                                 • Other central oculomotor abnormalities (central nystagmus, impaired smooth pursuit or saccades)
                                                                 • Increased risk for vascular events (atrial fibrillation, ABCD2 score of 4 or more)
                                                             • Not better accounted for by another disease or disorder
                                                         Transient
                                                             • Acute vertigo, dizziness, or unsteadiness lasting for more than 3 hours but not yet 24 hours
                                                             • At least one of the following:
                                                                 • Focal central neurologic signs and symptoms or severe ataxia
                                                                 • At least one component of the HINTS exam
                                                                 • Other central oculomotor abnormalities (central nystagmus, impaired smooth pursuit or saccades)
                                                                 • New onset of moderate to severe craniocervical pain
                                                                 • Increased risk for vascular events (atrial fibrillation, ABCD2 score of 4 or more)
                                                             • Not better accounted for by another disease or disorder
                                     • Other
                                         ✓• Vestibular migraine
                                             • The most common central vestibular disorder (1-2.7% of general population)
                                             • Characterized by episodic dizziness (minutes to hours)
                                                 • Internal vertigo (sensation of self-motion)
                                                 • External vertigo (sensation that visual surround is spinning)
                                                 • Positional vertigo, occurring with change in head position
                                                 • Visually-induced vertigo triggered by complex visual scene/stimulus
                                                 • Head motion-induced vertigo occurring during head motion
                                                 • Head motion-induced dizziness with nausea
                                             • Other symptoms
                                                 • Nausea/vomiting
                                                 • Transient auditory symptoms
                                                 • Unsteadiness
                                             (.a)------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                                .Vestibular Migraine: Diagnostic Criteria
                                                    • At least 5 episodes with vestibular symptoms of moderate or severe intensity lasting 5 minutes to 72 hours
                                                    • Current or previous history of migraine with or without aura according to the International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD)
                                                    • One or more migraine features with at least 50% of vestibular episodes
                                                        • Headache with at least 2 of the following:
                                                            • One sided location
                                                            • Pulsating quality
                                                            • Moderate or severe pain
                                                            • Aggravation by routine physical activity
                                                        • Photophobia or phonophobia
                                                        • Visual aura
                                                    • Not better accounted for by another vestibular or ICHD diagnosis
                                                    ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                                      .Vestibular Migraine of Childhood
                                                         • Episodic syndrome in children associated with migraine
                                                         • Five episodes of vestibular symptoms of moderate or severe intensity lasting between 5 minutes to 72 hours
                                                         • A current or past history of migraine with or without aura
                                                         • One or more migraine features with at least 50% of vestibular episodes
                                                             • Headache with at least 2 of the following:
                                                                 • One sided location
                                                                 • Pulsating quality
                                                                 • Moderate or severe pain
                                                                 • Aggravation by routine physical activity
                                                             • Photophobia or phonophobia
                                                             • Visual aura
                                                         • Age < 18 years
                                                         • Not better accounted for by another headache disorder, vestibular disorder, or other condition
                                                .Provoking Factors for Vestibular Migraine
                                                   • Lack of sleep
                                                   • Stress
                                                   • Menstruation
                                                   • Dehydration
                                                   • Food triggers
                                                       • Caffeine
                                                       • Additives/preservatives
                                                .Management for Vestibular Migraine
                                                   • Lifestyle modification
                                                       • Avoidance of triggers, balanced diet
                                                       • Staying hydrated
                                                       • Regular activity
                                                       • Sleep hygiene 
                                                       • Address medication overuse
                                                   • Pharmacological management
                                                       • Medications for acute headache events (abortive)
                                                       • Preventative medications
                                                   • Vestibular rehabilitation

                                             Γ(Comparisons with other diseases)------------------------------------------------------------------------------ (!!).Per donar constancia en les altres seccions
                                                .Vestibular Migraine vs. BPPV
                                                   • Vestibular migraine may present with positional vertigo, which mimics BPPV
                                                   • The positional nystagmus is usually persistent with a slower velocity than is consistent with the what one typically sees with classic BPPV
                                                   • Episodes of dizziness or vertigo due to vestibular migraine are usually more frequent than BPPV recurrences
                                                   • Complicating factor: BPPV is more common in patients with migraine
                                                       • Therefore, may be co-existing with vestibular migraine
                                                .Migraine and Meniere's Disease
                                                   • The overlap between the two conditions in some people makes diagnosis difficult
                                                   • Migraine is more common in persons with Meniere's Disease (MD) compared to healthy controls
                                                   • Pathophysiologic relationship between migraine and MD is uncertain
                                                   • Fluctuating hearing loss, aural pressure, tinnitus, photophobia and migraine auras can occur in both conditions 
                                                   • For diagnosis of both, the patient would need to meet the criteria for each condition separately
                                         ✓• Functional disorders (persistent postural perceptual dizziness) (PPPD)
                                         ✓• Psychiatric diagnoses
                                             ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                             .Functional and Psychiatric Disorders
                                                • Persistent postural perceptual dizziness (PPPD)
                                                   • Chronic vestibular condition
                                                   • Functional disorders: A change in the mode of action of an organ without structural change
                                                   • May be precipitated by structural vestibular and/or psychological disorders
                                                   • Generalized anxiety disorder
                                                   • Panic disorder
                                                   • Phobias
                                                   • Fear of falling
                                                   • Acrophobia
                                                   ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                                      .Common features of psychophysiological dizziness 1 
                                                         • Describe floating, swimming in head, spinning in head
                                                         • Complain of tension headaches, palpitations, gastric disorders
                                                         • Symptoms may be constant but are increased with stress, certain 
                                                         situations, hyperventilation, or cardiac arrhythmias
                                                         • May see syncope and/or paresthesia
                                                      .Common features of psychophysiological dizziness 2
                                                         • Features of panic attacks:
                                                             • Shortness of breath
                                                             • Choking
                                                             • Chest pain
                                                             • Nausea
                                                             • Shaking
                                                             • Fear of dying
                                                             • Loss of control
                                                             • Sweating
                                                             • Palpitations
                                                   ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                                                      .PPPD: Diagnostic Criteria
                                                          • One or more symptoms of dizziness, unsteadiness, or non-spinning vertigo are present on most days for 3 months or more
                                                              • Symptoms last for prolonged periods of time but may fluctuate in severity
                                                              • Symptoms need not be continuous throughout the day
                                                          • Persistent symptoms occur without specific provocation but are exacerbated by three factors:
                                                              • Upright posture
                                                              • Active or passive motion without regard to direction or position
                                                              • Exposure to moving visual stimuli or complex visual patterns
                                                          • The disorder is precipitated by conditions that cause vertigo, unsteadiness, or problems with balance (acute, episodic, or chronic vestibular syndromes, neurologic or medical illnesses, or psychological distress
                                                          • Symptoms cause significant distress or functional impairment
                                                          • Symptoms are not better accounted for by another disease or disorder
                                         ✓• Arnold-Chiari malformation
                                             .Chiari Malformation Signs and Symptoms
                                                • Headache
                                                • Neck pain
                                                • Vertigo
                                                • Balance problem
                                                • Weakness
                                                • Dysphagia
                                                • Downbeat nystagmus
                                                • Vertigo with neck extension
                                         • Tumor
                                 .Typical Central Signs and Symptoms
                                     • Cranial nerve signs
                                         • Changes in pupillary size
                                         • Ptosis
                                         • Difficulty with swallowing
                                     • Other neurologic signs
                                         • Downbeat nystagmus
                                         • Cerebellar signs and symptoms
                                         • Headaches 
                                         • Associated head injuries/cervical dysfunction
                                         • A sense of tilting by the patient
                                         • Changes in sensation
                                         • A positive Babinski, increased DTR’s, or clonus
                                         • Impaired gait/ataxia
                           • Combined peripheral/central disorders

                     Γ.Action Statements
                        .Action Statement 7: Effectiveness of supervised vestibular rehabilitation
                           • Clinicians should offer supervised vestibular physical therapy in individuals with unilateral or bilateral peripheral vestibular hypofunction. (Evidence Quality: I; Recommendation Strength: Strong)
                           • Evidence suggests that: 
                               oIndividuals drop out at higher rates when unsupervised 
                               oIndividuals older than 50 years of age may benefit more from supervision 
                               oIndividuals who are fearful of falling may not do well in an unsupervised program
                           • Regular in-person monitoring may be more beneficial than a remotely monitored HEP for individuals with UVH/BVH plus cognitive impairment
                        .Action Statement 8: Decision rules for stopping vestibular rehabilitation in individuals with peripheral vestibular hypofunction (unilateral and bilateral)
                            • Clinicians may use achievement of primary goals, resolution of symptoms, normalized balance and vestibular function, or plateau in progress as reasons for stopping therapy (Evidence Quality: II; Recommendation strength: Moderate)
                            • Ultimately, the individual decides whether to participate and when to stop
                            • Individuals with moderate to severe cognitive or mobility impairments may need additional treatment sessions.  
                                oThese individuals are often excluded in research, so stopping rules may not be appropriate for them
                        .Action Statement 9: factors that modify rehabilitation outcomes
                           • Clinicians may evaluate factors that could modify rehabilitation outcomes.
                              (Age: Evidence quality: I; Recommendation strength: Strong; Other Factors: Evidence quality: II; Recommendation strength: Moderate)
                                   oAge and gender do not affect rehabilitation potential for improvement
                                   oParticipation in vestibular exercises results in improved outcomes regardless 
                                   of time from onset in individuals with chronic UVH
                                       § Potential harm of delaying intervention warrants initiating rehabilitation as soon as possible
                                   oCertain co-morbidities (anxiety, depression, peripheral neuropathy, migraine, abnormal binocular vision, and abnormal cognition) may negatively impact rehabilitation outcomes. 
                                       § Consider co-morbidities when setting goals and refer to other healthcare professionals as appropriate
                              .FACTORS THAT MODIFY REHABILITATION OUTCOMES
                                  -Long-term use of vestibular suppressant medication may negatively impact an individual’s recovery
                                  -Short-term use of low-dose antihistamines in individuals with chronic vestibular disorders may help control symptoms during VPT without negative impact on outcomes
                                  -Exercise approaches should be designed to take these factors into account
                        .Action Statement 10: the harm/benefit ratio for vestibular rehabilitation in terms of quality of life
                            • Clinicians should offer vestibular physical therapy to persons with peripheral vestibular hypofunction with the intention of improving quality of life. (Evidence quality: Level I; Recommendation strength: Strong)
                                oImproved quality of life and psychological outcomes of individuals undergoing VPT compared to controls
                            • Nearly half of individuals with BVH changed their driving habits, reported reduced participation in social activities and difficulties of daily living: 
                                oClinical Pearl: PT evaluation, treatment, and education should include these common activities to help address quality of life
                        .Additional Clinical Pearls
                           -Risk of fall-related injury may last up to one year after acute UVH 
                           -Fall prevention education is imperative for this population!
                           -Use of a balance rating scale to measure perceived intensity of balance exercises may assist in appropriate modifications to balance exercises
                           -Use of a balance rating scale to measure perceived intensity of balance exercises may assist in appropriate modifications to balance exercises
