                        Absolutely. Based on a thorough review of all the documents you’ve provided — including `NM.txt`, `UpRuperta.txt`, and references to course materials like lab worksheets, clinical practice guidelines (CPG), case vignettes, and rubrics — I’ve compiled a comprehensive, organized list of what you need to be prepared for in your practical exam.

                        This list is designed to:
                        - Clarify the difference between Medical Diagnosis (MDx) and Physical Therapy Diagnosis (PT Dx)
                        - Show how they map to one another
                        - Highlight all possible cases that could appear on the practical
                        - Emphasize key distinctions (e.g., peripheral vs. central, emergent vs. non-emergent)
                        - Include red flags, referral criteria, and intervention appropriateness

                        Let’s begin.

                        ---

                        ## 1) ✅ All Possible Medical Diagnoses (MDx)  
                           (What the physician diagnoses — the underlying disease or pathology)

                           These are system-based and derived from your course materials, case vignettes, and lab documents.

                           ### A. Peripheral Vestibular Disorders
                              1. Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)  
                                 - Subtypes:  
                                   - Right/Left Posterior Canal BPPV  
                                   - Right/Left Horizontal (Lateral) Canal BPPV (geotropic or ageotropic)  
                              2. Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy (Vestibular Neuritis)  
                                 - Right or left side  
                              3. Labyrinthitis  
                                 - Right or left side (with hearing loss)  
                              4. Bilateral Vestibulopathy  
                                 - Often due to ototoxicity or autoimmune causes  

                           ### B. Central Vestibular Disorders
                              5. Cerebellar Stroke (Infarct or Hemorrhage)  
                                 - Right or left cerebellar hemisphere  
                              6. Brainstem Stroke (e.g., Vertebrobasilar Insufficiency)  
                              7. Multiple Sclerosis (MS) – with brainstem/cerebellar lesions  
                              8. Vestibular Migraine  
                              9. Cervicogenic Dizziness – controversial, but often included  
                              10. Acoustic Neuroma (Vestibular Schwannoma) – slow-growing tumor on CN VIII  

                           ### C. Other Neurological Conditions (Balance & Gait Impairments)
                              11. Parkinson’s Disease  
                              12. Stroke (Cerebrovascular Accident – CVA)  
                                 - Cortical (e.g., middle cerebral artery)  
                                 - Subcortical (e.g., internal capsule)  
                                 - Brainstem or cerebellar  
                              13. Spinal Cord Injury (SCI)  
                                 - Incomplete vs. complete  
                                 - Level-specific (cervical, thoracic)  
                              14. Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) / Concussion (mTBI)  
                              15. Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH)  
                              16. Progressive Supranuclear Palsy (PSP) or Multiple System Atrophy (MSA) – rare but testable  

                           ### D. Non-Vestibular Causes of Dizziness/Imbalance
                              17. Orthostatic Hypotension  
                              18. Cardiovascular Syncope / Arrhythmia  
                              19. Medication Side Effects (e.g., antihypertensives, benzodiazepines)  
                              20. Anxiety / Panic Disorder (functional dizziness)  

                        ---

                        ## 2) ✅ All Possible Physical Therapy Diagnoses (PT Dx)  
                           (What the PT diagnoses — the movement system impairments based on ICF model)

                           These are movement-based, derived from the Neurologic PT Framework, and organized by movement system categories.

                           ### A. Vestibular-Related PT Diagnoses
                              1. Impaired Static and Dynamic Postural Control associated with vestibular hypofunction  
                                 - E.g., after vestibular neuritis or BPPV  
                              2. Impaired Balance associated with abnormal vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR)  
                              3. Impaired Gait associated with vestibular dysfunction  
                              4. Impaired Head and Trunk Stability during functional activities  
                              5. Impaired Sensory Organization for Balance  
                                 - E.g., over-reliance on vision or somatosensation due to vestibular loss  

                           ### B. Motor Control & Coordination PT Diagnoses
                              6. Impaired Selective Motor Control associated with upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion  
                              7. Impaired Coordination / Ataxia associated with cerebellar dysfunction  
                              8. Impaired Motor Learning associated with central nervous system (CNS) disorder  
                              9. Impaired Neuromuscular Control associated with lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion  

                           ### C. Muscle Performance & Tone PT Diagnoses
                              10. Impaired Muscle Performance (Strength, Endurance, Power)  
                              11. Impaired Muscle Tone  
                                 - Spasticity (velocity-dependent) → UMN  
                                 - Rigidity (lead-pipe/cogwheel) → Parkinson’s  
                                 - Hypotonia → cerebellar or LMN  

                           ### D. Functional Mobility & Gait PT Diagnoses
                              12. Impaired Bed Mobility associated with neuromuscular dysfunction  
                              13. Impaired Sit-to-Stand Transfer associated with weakness or balance deficit  
                              14. Impaired Ambulation associated with ataxia, hypotonia, or sensory deficit  
                              15. Impaired Stair Negotiation associated with dynamic balance deficit  

                           ### E. Sensory & Perceptual PT Diagnoses
                              16. Impaired Proprioception associated with dorsal column dysfunction  
                              17. Impaired Sensation (Light Touch, Pain, Temp) associated with peripheral nerve or spinal cord lesion  
                              18. Impaired Oculomotor Control associated with brainstem or cerebellar dysfunction  

                           ### F. Cognitive-Motor Integration PT Diagnoses
                              19. Impaired Dual-Task Performance associated with CNS disorder  
                              20. Impaired Safety Awareness and Judgment associated with frontal lobe or diffuse brain injury  

                        > 🔍 Note: PT diagnoses are not "BPPV" or "stroke" — those are medical diagnoses.  
                        > The PT diagnosis describes the movement impairment (e.g., "Impaired dynamic postural control due to left vestibular hypofunction").

                        ---

                        ## 3) ✅ All Possible Cases for the Practical Exam  
                           (Based on frequency, emphasis in materials, and rubric focus)

                           Here are the most likely cases you’ll encounter, ranked by likelihood and importance.

                           ---

                           ### 🟩 High-Yield Cases (Very Likely to Appear)
                              #### Case 1: Right or Left Posterior Canal BPPV
                              - MDx: Left posterior canal BPPV  
                              - Key Test: Dix-Hallpike → torsional upbeating nystagmus with latency/fatigue  
                              - PT Dx: Impaired static/dynamic balance associated with positional vertigo  
                              - Intervention: Epley maneuver (canalith repositioning)  
                              - Red Flags: No hearing loss, no neurologic symptoms  
                              - Safety: Feet on ground during maneuver  
                              - HEP: Brandt-Daroff exercises, avoid affected side for 48h  

                              #### Case 2: Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy (Vestibular Neuritis)
                              - MDx: Left vestibular neuritis  
                              - Key Tests:  
                                - Head Impulse Test (HIT) → catch-up saccade on left  
                                - Spontaneous nystagmus → horizontal-torsional, beats to right (away from lesion)  
                                - Negative Dix-Hallpike  
                              - PT Dx: Impaired postural control due to unilateral vestibular hypofunction  
                              - Intervention: VOR adaptation exercises (e.g., gaze stabilization), habituation  
                              - Red Flags: No hearing loss → rules out labyrinthitis  
                              - Progression: Add dynamic balance, dual-task, walking with head turns  

                              #### Case 3: Central Vestibular Disorder (e.g., Cerebellar Stroke)
                              - MDx: Right cerebellar infarct  
                              - Key Findings:  
                                - Gait ataxia, truncal sway  
                                - Dysmetria (Finger-to-Nose, Heel-to-Shin)  
                                - Dysdiadochokinesia  
                                - Nystagmus: downbeating, gaze-evoked  
                                - Abnormal saccades/smooth pursuit  
                              - PT Dx: Impaired dynamic balance and coordination due to cerebellar dysfunction  
                              - Intervention: Balance retraining, coordination drills, gait training  
                              - Referral: Already confirmed — but you must rule out BPPV  
                              - Safety: High fall risk — use gait belt, supervise closely  

                              #### Case 4: Concussion / mTBI with Vestibulo-Ocular Dysfunction
                              - MDx: Mild Traumatic Brain Injury (mTBI)  
                              - Key Tool: VOMS (Vestibular/Ocular Motor Screening)  
                                - Smooth pursuit → saccadic  
                                - Saccades → dysmetric  
                                - VOR → symptom provocation  
                                - Convergence → near point recession  
                              - PT Dx: Impaired oculomotor control and dynamic balance post-concussion  
                              - Intervention: Sub-symptom threshold exercise, VOR retraining, dual-task training  
                              - Red Flags: Worsening headache, vomiting, pupillary changes → refer immediately  
                              - Progression: Gradual increase in exertion, avoid symptom provocation  

                           ---

                           ### 🟨 Medium-Yield Cases (Possible, but less frequent)
                              #### Case 5: Horizontal Canal BPPV (Geotropic vs. Ageotropic)
                              - MDx: Right horizontal canal BPPV, ageotropic  
                              - Key Test: Supine Roll Test → nystagmus beats toward ceiling (ageotropic)  
                              - PT Dx: Impaired balance with positional changes  
                              - Intervention: Barbecue (Lempert) roll or Gufoni maneuver  
                              - Why it’s testable: Differentiates from posterior canal BPPV  

                              #### Case 6: Bilateral Vestibulopathy
                              - MDx: Bilateral vestibular loss (e.g., ototoxicity)  
                              - Key Test: Bilateral positive HIT (catch-up saccades both sides)  
                              - PT Dx: Impaired balance in dark or on uneven surfaces  
                              - Intervention: Sensory substitution training, gait training with visual cues  
                              - Red Flags: Oscillopsia (bouncing vision with walking)  

                              #### Case 7: Parkinson’s Disease (with postural instability)
                              - MDx: Parkinson’s Disease  
                              - Key Findings:  
                                - Rigidity (cogwheel), bradykinesia  
                                - Postural instability, shuffling gait  
                                - Impaired reactive postural control  
                              - PT Dx: Impaired balance and gait due to basal ganglia dysfunction  
                              - Intervention: Cueing strategies, large amplitude movements, fall prevention  

                           ---

                           ### 🟥 Low-Yield but Possible (Know the red flags)
                              #### Case 8: Stroke (CVA) – Non-Vestibular
                              - MDx: Right MCA stroke  
                              - Key Findings: Left hemiparesis, spasticity, impaired coordination  
                              - PT Dx: Impaired ambulation due to hemiparesis and impaired motor control  
                              - Intervention: Gait training, strengthening, balance retraining  
                              - Red Flags: Sudden onset, facial droop, aphasia → already diagnosed  

                              #### Case 9: Spinal Cord Injury (SCI) – Sensory Ataxia
                              - MDx: Incomplete cervical SCI  
                              - Key Finding: Impaired proprioception → sensory ataxia  
                              - PT Dx: Impaired balance due to impaired joint position sense  
                              - Intervention: Weight shifting, balance on foam, visual feedback  

                              #### Case 10: Orthostatic Hypotension
                              - MDx: Autonomic dysfunction  
                              - Key Test: Orthostatic BP drop (>20 mmHg SBP or >10 mmHg DBP)  
                              - PT Dx: Impaired standing balance due to cardiovascular instability  
                              - Intervention: Education, slow position changes, compression garments  
                              - Red Flag: Dizziness on standing → must rule out before vestibular testing

                        ## 🔍 Final Tips for Practical Exam Success

                           | Area                  | What to Focus On                                                                         |
                           |-----------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
                           | Chart Review      | Always ask: PLF, social history, fall history, meds, red flags                       |
                           | History Questions | Use HPI structure: Onset, Quality, Duration, Triggers, Associated Sx, Course         |
                           | PT Exam           | Prioritize: Cranial Nerves (II, III, IV, VI, VIII), VOMS, Balance, Coordination      |
                           | Test & Measure    | Know: Dix-Hallpike, HIT, VOMS, Romberg, FGA, BBS                                     |
                           | Interpretation    | Explain why the finding matters (e.g., "Catch-up saccade = vestibular hypofunction") |
                           | Intervention      | Specify side, dosage, progression criteria (e.g., symptoms <3/10)                    |
                           | Safety            | Feet on ground, gait belt, no excessive cueing                                       |
                           | Education         | Be specific: "Do Epley 3x/day for 2 weeks", "Avoid rolling onto left side"           |

                        ### ✅ So far, here are the three simulation cases we’ve covered:

                        ---

                        #### 1. Case: Ruperta M. → Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)  
                        - Medical Diagnosis: Left Posterior Canal BPPV  
                        - Category: Peripheral Vestibular – Positional Vertigo  
                        - Key Features:
                          - Episodic vertigo with position changes (bending over, rolling in bed)
                          - Lasts <30 seconds
                          - Torsional upbeating nystagmus on left Dix-Hallpike
                          - Latency, fatigability, crescendo-decrescendo pattern
                        - Critical Test: Dix-Hallpike Maneuver
                        - Critical Intervention: Epley Maneuver (Canalith Repositioning)
                        - PT Diagnosis:  
                          - Impaired static and dynamic postural control associated with positional vertigo
                        - Why It’s Important:
                          - Most common cause of vertigo
                          - Highly treatable with manual therapy
                          - You were marked down on HIT interpretation, safety (feet), and education — so we focused on precision

                        > 🔁 Contrast: Unlike AUVP or stroke, BPPV is not constant, and VOR is normal.

                        ---

                        #### 2. Case: Mr. Elias → Right Cerebellar Infarct (Central Vestibular Disorder)  
                        - Medical Diagnosis: Acute Right Cerebellar Infarct  
                        - Category: Central Vestibular – Cerebellar Ataxia  
                        - Key Features:
                          - Sudden onset of constant dizziness and imbalance
                          - No hearing loss
                          - Positive fall history
                          - On exam: gait ataxia, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, intention tremor
                          - Nystagmus: downbeating or gaze-evoked
                        - Critical Tests:
                          - Finger-to-Nose (FTN), Heel-to-Shin (HTS), Rapid Alternating Movements (RAM)
                          - Abnormal saccades and smooth pursuit
                          - Normal HIT (unlike vestibular neuritis)
                        - Critical Intervention: Balance retraining, coordination drills, gait training with dual-task
                        - PT Diagnosis:  
                          - Impaired dynamic balance and coordination associated with cerebellar dysfunction
                        - Why It’s Important:
                          - Mimics peripheral vertigo but is medical emergency
                          - Requires different treatment (no Epley!)
                          - High fall risk — safety is paramount

                        > 🔁 Contrast: Unlike BPPV, vertigo is constant, not positional. Unlike AUVP, VOR is normal, but oculomotor control is impaired.

                        #### 3. Case: Mrs. Amalia → Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy (AUVP / Vestibular Neuritis)  
                        - Medical Diagnosis: Left Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy  
                        - Category: Peripheral Vestibular – Vestibular Hypofunction
                        - Key Features:
                          - Sudden onset of constant spinning vertigo lasting days
                          - Nausea, imbalance, worse with head movement
                          - No hearing loss (rules out labyrinthitis)
                          - Spontaneous nystagmus: horizontal-torsional, beats to the right (away from lesion)
                          - Positive Head Impulse Test (HIT): catch-up saccade to the left
                          - Negative Dix-Hallpike (rules out BPPV)
                        - Critical Tests:
                          - Head Impulse Test (HIT)
                          - Spontaneous nystagmus observation
                          - VOMS (normal saccades, smooth pursuit)
                        - Critical Intervention: VOR Adaptation Exercises (VORx1, VORx2), habituation, balance retraining
                        - PT Diagnosis:  
                          - Impaired postural control and dynamic balance associated with unilateral vestibular hypofunction
                        - Why It’s Important:
                          - Most common cause of acute spontaneous vertigo
                          - Requires early vestibular rehab for optimal recovery
                          - Often misdiagnosed as BPPV or stroke

                        > 🔁 Contrast: Unlike BPPV, it’s not positional. Unlike cerebellar stroke, coordination is normal.

                     .Make a review of the differences between the cases .Patient Case 4 Γ(Posterior Canal BPPV), .Patient Case 6 Γ(Horizontal (Lateral) Canal BPPV (geotropic)), .Patient Case 8 Γ(Horizontal (Lateral) Canal BPPV (ageotropic)), .Patient Case 10 Γ(Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy (Vestibular Neuritis)), .Patient Case 12 Γ(Labyrinthitis), and .Patient Case 14 Γ(Bilateral Vestibulopathy). I want to have an overview of how to structure the exams. Do not make lists of elements, just text paragraphs.
                        When approaching a patient with dizziness, the key to accurate diagnosis lies in a structured, systematic evaluation that integrates history, observation, and targeted testing to differentiate between peripheral vestibular disorders. Each of the cases—Posterior Canal BPPV, Horizontal Canal BPPV (geotropic and apogeotropic), Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy, Labyrinthitis, and Bilateral Vestibulopathy—presents with vertigo or imbalance, but the pattern of symptoms, timing, and response to positional testing are distinct, guiding the clinician toward the correct diagnosis.

                        In Posterior Canal BPPV, the hallmark is brief, intense episodes of vertigo triggered by changes in head position relative to gravity, such as rolling in bed or looking up. The history typically reveals episodic, position-dependent dizziness lasting seconds, which fatigues with repetition. The Dix-Hallpike maneuver is diagnostic, producing a characteristic torsional-upbeating nystagmus with a latency of a few seconds, peaking within 20–30 seconds, and then fatiguing. The direction of the torsional component (toward the lower ear) confirms the affected side. This contrasts sharply with Horizontal (Lateral) Canal BPPV, where vertigo is provoked by side-lying movements, and the Supine Roll Test elicits horizontal nystagmus. In the geotropic variant, the nystagmus beats toward the earth (downward ear), indicating free-floating debris (canalithiasis), and the intensity is greater when lying on the affected side. This guides the use of repositioning maneuvers like the Gufoni or Li Quick. In contrast, the apogeotropic variant presents with nystagmus beating away from the earth, often suggesting cupulolithiasis (otoconia adhered to the cupula), and the affected side is identified by the less intense nystagmus when lying on that side—a counterintuitive finding that requires careful interpretation. The Kim maneuver is the first-line treatment here.

                        Moving beyond BPPV, Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy (Vestibular Neuritis) presents a very different picture: a sudden, constant vertigo lasting days, accompanied by nausea and imbalance, but not triggered by position changes. There is no latency or fatigability. The spontaneous nystagmus is horizontal-torsional, beating away from the affected side, and follows Alexander’s law (increases with gaze toward the fast phase). The Head Impulse Test (HIT) is positive on the affected side, showing a corrective saccade, while the Dix-Hallpike and Supine Roll tests are negative. This is a diagnosis of peripheral hypofunction, not mechanical displacement, so canalith repositioning is inappropriate. Instead, early vestibular rehabilitation focusing on VOR adaptation and habituation is key.

                        When hearing symptoms are present—sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus—the diagnosis shifts to Labyrinthitis, which involves both the vestibular and cochlear divisions of the 8th nerve. The vestibular exam mirrors vestibular neuritis (spontaneous nystagmus, positive HIT), but the addition of hearing loss, confirmed by whispered voice test, Rinne, and Weber, is the critical differentiator. This distinction is vital, as it affects prognosis and management, though the initial PT approach to vestibular rehab remains similar.

                        Finally, Bilateral Vestibulopathy presents not with vertigo, but with chronic imbalance, particularly in the dark or on uneven surfaces, and oscillopsia—the sensation that the world bounces with head movement. There is no spontaneous nystagmus, and the HIT is bilaterally abnormal. The Dynamic Visual Acuity (DVA) test shows a significant loss of acuity with head movement. The mCTSIB reveals profound difficulty with Condition 4 (eyes closed on foam). Unlike the other conditions, there is no asymmetry to drive vertigo; instead, the brain lacks vestibular input on both sides. The history often includes ototoxic medication exposure (e.g., gentamicin) or autoimmune disease. PT focuses on substitution strategies, enhancing reliance on vision and somatosensation, rather than repositioning maneuvers.

                        The structure of the exam flows from this differential. It begins with a detailed history to determine if the dizziness is episodic/positional (BPPV), acute/constant (neuritis/labyrinthitis), or chronic/imbalance-dominant (bilateral loss). Observation for gait and head posture provides immediate clues. The exam then systematically rules out BPPV using the Dix-Hallpike and Supine Roll tests. If negative, attention turns to spontaneous nystagmus, HIT, and hearing to differentiate neuritis from labyrinthitis. If no nystagmus is present, bilateral vestibulopathy is suspected, confirmed by HIT bilaterally and DVA. Throughout, safety, prior function, and patient goals are integrated to ensure a patient-centered, evidence-based approach.

                           ### 🟩 Patient Case 4: Right Posterior Canal BPPV

                           | Question | What It Screens For | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |--------|---------------------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | “When did your dizziness start, and what were you doing at the time?” | Onset pattern (acute vs. insidious), potential trauma | Helps differentiate BPPV (often sudden with movement) from central or progressive causes | If onset was post-traumatic, it may change prognosis and recurrence risk; missing trauma history delays appropriate counseling |
                           | “Does the dizziness happen only with certain head movements, like lying down, rolling over, or looking up?” | Positional triggers | BPPV is episodic and positionally provoked; vertigo lasting >1 minute suggests non-BPPV etiology | This is the hallmark of BPPV — if not asked, you may misdiagnose it as vestibular neuritis or anxiety |
                           | “How long does each episode last?” | Duration of symptoms | BPPV episodes typically last 5–30 seconds; longer duration suggests central or Meniere’s pathology | Duration is diagnostic: >1 minute rules out typical BPPV and should prompt further investigation |
                           | “Does the spinning sensation go away if you stay still?” | Fatigability | BPPV nystagmus and vertigo fatigue with repetition; non-fatiguing nystagmus suggests central lesion | Fatigability supports canalithiasis; lack of fatigue raises concern for cupulolithiasis or central cause |
                           | “Do you feel unsteady between episodes, or only during the spinning?” | Inter-episodic imbalance | BPPV causes no persistent imbalance; ongoing unsteadiness suggests vestibular hypofunction or central pathology | Persistent imbalance is a red flag — indicates another diagnosis (e.g., neuritis, stroke) coexisting or misdiagnosis |
                           | “Have you had any recent head injuries or falls?” | Post-traumatic BPPV | Up to 15% of BPPV cases are post-traumatic; trauma increases recurrence risk | Missing this may lead to underestimating recurrence and inadequate patient education on prevention |
                           | “Do you have any hearing changes, tinnitus, or fullness in your ears?” | Cochlear involvement | Hearing symptoms suggest labyrinthitis or Meniere’s, not isolated BPPV | If present, BPPV is less likely; you must rule out more serious or mixed diagnoses |
                           | “Are you currently taking any vestibular suppressants (e.g., meclizine, diazepam)?” | Medication effects | These delay central compensation and may mask symptoms | Patients on suppressants may appear less symptomatic during testing, leading to false-negative results |
                           | “What activities are you avoiding because of the dizziness?” | Functional impact and kinesiophobia | Identifies fear of movement and activity restriction | Fear of rolling in bed or driving can severely limit quality of life; this guides home program and education |
                           | “Do you live alone or with someone who can help you if you fall?” | Safety and support system | Assesses fall risk and ability to respond to acute episodes | BPPV increases fall risk during positional changes; living alone increases danger if syncope or prolonged vertigo occurs |

                           ### 🟨 Patient Case 6: Left Horizontal (Lateral) Canal BPPV (Geotropic)

                           | Question | What It Screens For | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |--------|---------------------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | “Does your dizziness occur mainly when you roll onto your left or right side in bed?” | Lateral canal involvement | Horizontal canal BPPV is triggered by side-lying positions, unlike posterior canal | This is the primary differentiator — if not asked, you may perform Dix-Hallpike unnecessarily and miss HC-BPPV |
                           | “Which side makes the dizziness worse — left or right?” | Affected side determination | In geotropic HC-BPPV, vertigo and nystagmus are more intense when lying on the affected side | This is counterintuitive to apogeotropic; misinterpreting intensity leads to wrong maneuver and treatment failure |
                           | “Is the dizziness spinning, and does it come on quickly when you move?” | Quality and latency | Geotropic BPPV has short latency (seconds) and horizontal nystagmus beating toward the lower ear | Helps distinguish from central nystagmus (no latency, persistent) or cervicogenic dizziness (non-spinning) |
                           | “Do you feel worse when lying flat on your back and turning your head side to side?” | Supine Roll Test relevance | This is the provocative movement for horizontal canal BPPV | If patient reports this as worst trigger, it strongly supports HC-BPPV and justifies performing the roll test |
                           | “Have you noticed if the dizziness gets better after repeating the movement?” | Fatigability | Geotropic HC-BPPV due to canalithiasis typically fatigues with repetition | Lack of fatigability suggests cupulolithiasis (apogeotropic), requiring a different treatment approach |
                           | “Do you have any neck pain or stiffness when moving your head?” | Cervicogenic mimic | Neck pain may suggest alternative or coexisting diagnosis | Cervical spine dysfunction can cause dizziness with head turn; must rule out to avoid misdiagnosis |
                           | “Have you ever had BPPV before, or been treated for it?” | Recurrence and treatment history | BPPV has high recurrence (30–50% within 1 year); prior treatment informs prognosis | If previously treated with Epley, but now has horizontal symptoms, may have canal conversion — important for maneuver selection |
                           | “Are you able to sleep on both sides, or do you avoid one side?” | Behavioral adaptation and kinesiophobia | Avoidance of one side indicates learned fear and functional limitation | This guides patient education and need for habituation strategies post-treatment |
                           | “Have you had any recent infections or illnesses?” | Post-viral BPPV | Viral illness may predispose to otoconial dislodgement | Not diagnostic, but supports benign etiology over central or structural causes |
                           | “Do you feel the world is bouncing when you walk?” | Oscillopsia | Absence of oscillopsia supports BPPV; presence suggests vestibular hypofunction | Oscillopsia is not seen in BPPV — if present, consider bilateral or unilateral vestibular loss instead |

                           ### 🟨 Patient Case 8: Left Horizontal (Lateral) Canal BPPV (Apogeotropic)

                           | Question | What It Screens For | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |--------|---------------------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | “When you lie down to one side, which side causes the strongest dizziness?” | Affected side in apogeotropic BPPV | In apogeotropic HC-BPPV, the nystagmus is less intense when lying on the affected side (cupulolithiasis) | This is inversely intuitive — if you assume worse side = affected side, you’ll treat the wrong ear and worsen symptoms |
                           | “Does the dizziness seem to last longer than typical BPPV episodes?” | Duration and persistence | Apogeotropic nystagmus is often persistent or slowly fatiguing due to cupulolithiasis | Prolonged symptoms suggest cupulolithiasis, which requires Kim maneuver, not Gufoni to unaffected side |
                           | “Do you feel dizzy even when lying still on one side?” | Persistent positional nystagmus | Cupulolithiasis causes non-fatiguing, persistent nystagmus | This differentiates it from geotropic (canalithiasis), which fatigues; guides treatment selection |
                           | “Have you ever had a head injury or fall recently?” | Post-traumatic etiology | Head trauma is a common cause of cupulolithiasis due to otoconia adhering to cupula | Trauma history increases likelihood of apogeotropic type and recurrence risk |
                           | “Do you notice dizziness when you bow your head forward or look up?” | Bow and Lean Test relevance | Apogeotropic BPPV may show transient nystagmus with head pitch | Bow and Lean Test helps confirm cupulolithiasis — essential for accurate diagnosis |
                           | “Has anyone told you your eyes are moving when you’re dizzy?” | Nystagmus observation | Apogeotropic nystagmus beats away from the lower ear (upward) | Patient may not see it, but family might — this supports diagnosis when exam is equivocal |
                           | “Have you had BPPV treatment before, like the Epley maneuver?” | Canal conversion risk | Prior posterior canal treatment can convert to horizontal canal BPPV | If so, apogeotropic HC-BPPV may be iatrogenic — informs treatment approach and patient education |
                           | “Do you feel unsteady during the day, even when not moving your head?” | Inter-episodic imbalance | Persistent imbalance suggests central compensation failure or misdiagnosis | Apogeotropic BPPV should not cause daily imbalance; presence suggests vestibular hypofunction |
                           | “Are you taking any medications that affect your balance?” | Ototoxic or CNS-depressant drugs | Medications like anticonvulsants or benzodiazepines can mimic or worsen dizziness | May confound symptoms and delay recovery; must be reviewed before attributing to BPPV |
                           | “Do you have any history of Meniere’s disease or hearing problems?” | Mixed vestibular-cochlear pathology | Hearing symptoms suggest alternative diagnosis | Apogeotropic BPPV is purely vestibular; hearing loss suggests labyrinthitis or Meniere’s |

                           ### 🟥 Patient Case 10: Left Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy (Vestibular Neuritis)

                           | Question | What It Screens For | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |--------|---------------------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | “Did the dizziness start suddenly, and was it constant from the beginning?” | Acute onset and persistence | Vestibular neuritis presents with sudden, continuous vertigo lasting days | This differentiates it from BPPV (episodic) and migraine (intermittent); key for diagnosis |
                           | “Do you feel nauseous or vomit with the dizziness?” | Autonomic symptoms | Severe nausea/vomiting is common in acute vestibular loss due to vestibular nuclei disruption | Helps distinguish from psychogenic or cervicogenic dizziness, which rarely cause vomiting |
                           | “Is the dizziness worse with head movement, even small ones?” | Movement sensitivity | UVH causes movement-provoked vertigo due to asymmetric VOR | This is hallmark of peripheral hypofunction; absence suggests central or non-vestibular cause |
                           | “Do you feel like the room is spinning, or more like lightheadedness?” | Quality of dizziness | True spinning vertigo indicates peripheral vestibular lesion | Lightheadedness suggests presyncope, anxiety, or medication side effect — different pathway |
                           | “Have you noticed any hearing changes, ringing, or fullness in your left ear?” | Cochlear nerve involvement | Hearing loss suggests labyrinthitis, not vestibular neuritis | This is the key differentiator — if present, diagnosis shifts to labyrinthitis |
                           | “Do you feel unsteady when walking, especially in the dark?” | Dynamic imbalance | UVH causes gait ataxia due to loss of vestibular input | Assesses functional impact and need for balance retraining |
                           | “Have you had any recent viral illness, like a cold or flu?” | Post-viral etiology | Vestibular neuritis is often post-viral (e.g., herpes family) | Supports diagnosis and informs patient that it’s not contagious or dangerous |
                           | “Are you taking any medications for the dizziness?” | Vestibular suppressant use | Meclizine, diazepam, etc., delay central compensation | You may recommend tapering them to promote faster recovery |
                           | “Can you walk without support, or do you need to hold onto walls?” | Functional mobility | Identifies fall risk and need for assistive device | Patients with UVH often require a cane initially; safety is paramount |
                           | “Do you live alone or with someone who can help during acute episodes?” | Safety and supervision | Acute UVH increases fall risk due to imbalance and vertigo | Living alone increases risk of injury; may require home modifications or temporary support |

                           ### 🟥 Patient Case 12: Left Labyrinthitis

                           | Question | What It Screens For | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |--------|---------------------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | “Have you noticed any hearing loss or ringing in your left ear?” | Cochlear involvement | Hearing loss + vertigo = labyrinthitis until proven otherwise | This is the defining feature — missing it leads to misdiagnosis as vestibular neuritis |
                           | “Is the tinnitus constant, or does it come and go?” | Pattern of cochlear symptoms | Constant tinnitus supports acute inflammatory process | Fluctuating tinnitus suggests Meniere’s disease — different management |
                           | “Did the hearing loss happen suddenly?” | Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL) | SSNHL is a medical emergency; may require steroids | If untreated within 72 hours, recovery is less likely — urgent referral may be needed |
                           | “Do you feel fullness or pressure in your left ear?” | Ménière’s mimic | Ear fullness can occur in both labyrinthitis and Meniere’s | Helps differentiate; Meniere’s has episodic vertigo, fluctuating hearing |
                           | “Have you had a recent ear infection or cold?” | Infectious etiology | Viral or bacterial infection can trigger labyrinthitis | Supports diagnosis and informs patient about expected recovery timeline |
                           | “Are you currently on steroids or antibiotics?” | Medical management | Steroids (e.g., prednisone) improve recovery in labyrinthitis | Knowing this helps coordinate care and avoid conflicting advice |
                           | “Is the vertigo constant, or does it come in spells?” | Duration and pattern | Labyrinthitis causes constant vertigo for days, unlike Meniere’s | Duration helps differentiate from other episodic disorders |
                           | “Do you feel worse with head movement?” | Vestibular hypofunction | Yes — due to asymmetric vestibular input | Confirms peripheral vestibular involvement, not central or psychogenic |
                           | “Have you had any dizziness before, or is this your first episode?” | Recurrence | Recurrent episodes suggest Meniere’s or autoimmune inner ear disease | First-time episode more likely post-viral; guides prognosis |
                           | “Are you able to hear whispers or the TV on the affected side?” | Functional hearing loss | Assesses severity of sensorineural loss | Guides need for audiology referral and patient safety (e.g., phone use, alarms) |

                           ### 🟦 Patient Case 14: Bilateral Vestibulopathy

                           | Question | What It Screens For | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |--------|---------------------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | “Do you feel unsteady when walking, especially in the dark or on uneven ground?” | Sensory dependence | BVH patients rely heavily on vision and somatosensation; imbalance worsens when these are removed | This is pathognomonic — if patient says yes, BVH is high on the differential |
                           | “Does the world seem to bounce when you walk or ride in a car?” | Oscillopsia | Caused by absent VOR — images slip on retina during head movement | This is a cardinal symptom of BVH; not seen in BPPV or neuritis |
                           | “Have you taken any medications like gentamicin, cisplatin, or loop diuretics?” | Ototoxic exposure | These drugs are common causes of bilateral vestibular loss | Missing this may prevent identification of cause and recurrence prevention |
                           | “Do you have difficulty seeing clearly when your head is moving?” | Dynamic visual acuity impairment | Due to failed VOR; measurable with DVA test | Confirms vestibular contribution to visual symptoms |
                           | “Is your imbalance gradual and long-standing, rather than sudden?” | Chronicity | BVH is chronic, not acute; develops over months to years | Acute onset suggests bilateral neuritis (rare) or toxic exposure |
                           | “Do you have a history of autoimmune disease or meningitis?” | Systemic causes | Autoimmune, infectious, or inflammatory conditions can cause BVH | Broadens differential and may require medical workup |
                           | “Do you feel more stable when holding onto something or using a cane?” | Sensory substitution | Patients with BVH improve with tactile input | Indicates need for assistive device and balance retraining |
                           | “Are you able to walk in a straight line with your eyes closed?” | Romberg and mCTSIB relevance | Likely positive Romberg (eyes closed sway) and failed mCTSIB Condition 4 | This is a key clinical sign — absence of vestibular input |
                           | “Have you had frequent falls, especially in low light?” | Fall risk | BVH increases fall risk due to poor dynamic balance | Critical for safety planning and home modification |
                           | “Do you avoid walking in grocery stores or crowded places?” | Visual motion sensitivity | Due to sensory conflict — visual motion overwhelms impaired vestibular system | Guides vestibular rehab focus on visual-vestibular integration |

                           ### 🔹 1. “When did your dizziness start, and what were you doing at the time?”

                           | Case | What It Screens For | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |------|---------------------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | Posterior Canal BPPV
                              | Timing and triggering event 
                                 | BPPV typically begins suddenly with a positional change (e.g., rolling in bed, getting up)
                                    | Helps distinguish from central or progressive causes; confirms mechanical, gravity-dependent etiology |
                           | Horizontal Canal BPPV (Geotropic)
                              | Onset during side-lying movement
                                 | Often starts when rolling to one side in bed, especially after head trauma or prolonged supine positioning
                                    | Identifies lateral canal involvement; guides use of Supine Roll Test over Dix-Hallpike |
                           | Horizontal Canal BPPV (Apogeotropic)
                              | Sudden onset with head motion or post-procedure
                                 | May follow head trauma, surgery, or prior BPPV treatment (canal conversion)
                                    | Trauma or iatrogenic onset supports cupulolithiasis; informs treatment selection (Kim maneuver) |
                           | Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy
                              | Abrupt, spontaneous onset
                                 | Neuritis begins without trigger, often upon waking, with constant vertigo
                                    | Sudden spontaneous onset + constant vertigo = hallmark of UVH; differentiates from episodic BPPV |
                           | Labyrinthitis
                              | Acute onset with or without prodromal illness
                                 | Typically sudden, like neuritis, but may follow viral upper respiratory infection
                                    | Onset pattern supports post-viral etiology; hearing symptoms confirm cochlear involvement |
                           | Bilateral Vestibulopathy
                              | Gradual, insidious onset over months/years
                                 | BVH develops slowly; patient may not recall exact onset
                                    | Chronicity rules out acute peripheral causes; points to ototoxic, autoimmune, or degenerative etiology |

                           ---

                           ### 🔹 2. “Does the dizziness happen only with certain head movements?”

                           | Case | What It Screens For | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |------|---------------------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | Posterior Canal BPPV | Positional triggers (lying back, rolling, looking up) | Vertigo is strictly provoked by gravity-dependent head movements | This is diagnostic — if dizziness occurs at rest, BPPV is unlikely |
                           | Horizontal Canal BPPV (Geotropic) | Side-lying or head-turning triggers | Triggered by rolling onto either side; worse on affected side | Confirms lateral canal involvement; differentiates from posterior canal BPPV |
                           | Horizontal Canal BPPV (Apogeotropic) | Side-lying positions, but may persist | Triggered by lying down, but nystagmus may not fatigue due to cupulolithiasis | Persistent symptoms suggest cupulolithiasis, requiring different treatment (Kim vs. Gufoni) |
                           | Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy | Movement sensitivity (any head motion) | Dizziness is worsened by all head movements, not just positional changes | Helps differentiate from BPPV; indicates constant vestibular asymmetry |
                           | Labyrinthitis | General movement sensitivity | Like neuritis, worsened by any head motion, not just specific positions | Supports peripheral vestibular loss, not mechanical displacement |
                           | Bilateral Vestibulopathy | Walking or head motion (oscillopsia) | Not positional; worse during dynamic activities like walking or in cars | Oscillopsia with motion is pathognomonic; absence of positional trigger rules out BPPV |

                           ---

                           ### 🔹 3. “How long does each episode of dizziness last?”

                           | Case | What It Screens For | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |------|---------------------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | Posterior Canal BPPV | Duration of vertigo (5–30 seconds) | BPPV episodes are brief and self-limiting | Duration >30 sec suggests central or Meniere’s; <5 sec may be benign paroxysmal torticollis |
                           | Horizontal Canal BPPV (Geotropic) | Short duration (10–45 seconds) | Canalithiasis causes fatiguing, transient nystagmus | Duration helps confirm diagnosis; longer duration suggests cupulolithiasis |
                           | Horizontal Canal BPPV (Apogeotropic) | Longer or persistent nystagmus | Cupulolithiasis leads to non-fatiguing or slowly fatiguing nystagmus | Prolonged duration is a key differentiator; requires different treatment approach |
                           | Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy | Constant vertigo lasting days | Symptoms are continuous for 72+ hours, gradually improving | Duration distinguishes it from BPPV; constant vertigo = peripheral hypofunction |
                           | Labyrinthitis | Constant vertigo for several days | Similar to neuritis — lasts 3–7 days, then gradually improves | Duration supports acute peripheral loss; fluctuating duration suggests Meniere’s |
                           | Bilateral Vestibulopathy | No episodic vertigo; chronic imbalance | Imbalance is persistent, not episodic; no spinning sensation | Absence of episodic vertigo rules out BPPV; confirms chronic vestibular failure |

                           ---

                           ### 🔹 4. “Does the dizziness go away if you stay still?”

                           | Case | What It Screens For | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |------|---------------------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | Posterior Canal BPPV | Fatigability with repetition | Yes — symptoms fatigue with repeated positioning | Fatigability supports canalithiasis; lack of fatigue raises concern for central lesion |
                           | Horizontal Canal BPPV (Geotropic) | Fatigability of nystagmus | Yes — nystagmus diminishes with repeated rolls | Confirms free-floating debris; guides repositioning strategy |
                           | Horizontal Canal BPPV (Apogeotropic) | Lack of fatigability | No — nystagmus persists or slowly fatigues due to cupulolithiasis | Critical for diagnosis; non-fatiguing nystagmus = cupulolithiasis → Kim maneuver |
                           | Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy | Persistent vertigo at rest | No — vertigo is constant even at rest, improves slowly over days | Helps differentiate from BPPV; confirms vestibular nerve inflammation |
                           | Labyrinthitis | Constant vertigo at rest | No — like neuritis, vertigo persists at rest | Confirms acute peripheral loss; distinguishes from episodic disorders |
                           | Bilateral Vestibulopathy | No vertigo, but persistent imbalance | Not applicable — no vertigo; imbalance is constant | Reinforces diagnosis of chronic vestibular failure, not episodic dysfunction |

                           ---

                           ### 🔹 5. “Do you feel unsteady between episodes, or only during the spinning?”

                           | Case | What It Screens For | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |------|---------------------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | Posterior Canal BPPV | Inter-episodic stability | No — patient is completely normal between episodes | Persistent imbalance suggests alternative diagnosis (e.g., UVH, central) |
                           | Horizontal Canal BPPV (Geotropic) | Stability between positional episodes | No — symptom-free when still | If imbalance persists, consider canal conversion or compensation failure |
                           | Horizontal Canal BPPV (Apogeotropic) | Possible residual imbalance | Sometimes — due to persistent cupular deviation | May explain why some patients report lingering unsteadiness |
                           | Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy | Persistent imbalance | Yes — constant imbalance due to unilateral hypofunction | This is expected; guides need for vestibular rehab and gait training |
                           | Labyrinthitis | Ongoing imbalance | Yes — imbalance persists during acute phase and may take weeks to resolve | Indicates need for balance retraining and compensation strategies |
                           | Bilateral Vestibulopathy | Chronic, daily imbalance | Yes — constant unsteadiness, especially in dark or on foam | This is the primary complaint; guides use of mCTSIB and sensory reweighting |

                           ---

                           ### 🔹 6. “Have you noticed any hearing changes, tinnitus, or ear fullness?”

                           | Case | What It Screens For | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |------|---------------------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | Posterior Canal BPPV | Cochlear symptoms | No — BPPV is purely vestibular | Hearing symptoms suggest alternative diagnosis (e.g., Meniere’s, labyrinthitis) |
                           | Horizontal Canal BPPV (Geotropic) | Hearing involvement | No — isolated vestibular disorder | Presence of hearing loss requires audiology referral and rules out BPPV |
                           | Horizontal Canal BPPV (Apogeotropic) | Hearing symptoms | No — unless coexisting pathology | Hearing changes suggest labyrinthitis or Meniere’s, not isolated BPPV |
                           | Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy | Hearing preservation | No hearing loss — vestibular nerve only | Hearing loss would shift diagnosis to labyrinthitis |
                           | Labyrinthitis | Sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus | Yes — cochlear and vestibular involvement | This is the defining feature; confirms diagnosis and may require steroids |
                           | Bilateral Vestibulopathy | Hearing loss (ototoxic cause) | Yes — if caused by aminoglycosides, cisplatin, etc. | Ototoxic meds often affect both cochlea and vestibular system; critical for history |

                           ---

                           ### 🔹 7. “Do you feel like the world is bouncing when you walk?” (Oscillopsia)

                           | Case | What It Screens For | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |------|---------------------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | Posterior Canal BPPV | Visual motion disturbance | No — oscillopsia is not present in BPPV | If present, suggests vestibular hypofunction, not BPPV |
                           | Horizontal Canal BPPV (Geotropic) | Dynamic visual blurring | No — VOR intact between episodes | Oscillopsia would indicate additional vestibular loss |
                           | Horizontal Canal BPPV (Apogeotropic) | Visual instability | Rare — unless chronic or bilateral | Persistent oscillopsia suggests incomplete compensation or bilateral involvement |
                           | Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy | Transient oscillopsia | Yes — during acute phase, due to impaired VOR | Resolves with compensation; guides VOR adaptation exercises |
                           | Labyrinthitis | Oscillopsia with head movement | Yes — due to combined cochlear and vestibular loss | Confirms peripheral hypofunction; impacts rehab focus |
                           | Bilateral Vestibulopathy | Severe oscillopsia with walking or head motion | Yes — hallmark symptom due to absent VOR | This is diagnostic; guides use of DVA test and visual-vestibular training |

                           ---

                           ### 🔹 8. “Are you taking any medications for dizziness?”

                           | Case | What It Screens For | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |------|---------------------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | Posterior Canal BPPV | Vestibular suppressants | Meclizine, diazepam may mask symptoms | Suppressants delay compensation; should be tapered to allow effective testing |
                           | Horizontal Canal BPPV (Geotropic) | Medication effects | May reduce nystagmus intensity, leading to false-negative test | Must know med use to interpret test results accurately |
                           | Horizontal Canal BPPV (Apogeotropic) | Drug-induced dizziness | Some meds mimic BPPV or delay recovery | Important for differential; e.g., anticonvulsants cause ataxia |
                           | Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy | Suppressant use | Commonly prescribed; delays central compensation | You may recommend tapering within 72 hours to promote faster recovery |
                           | Labyrinthitis | Steroid or antibiotic use | Prednisone may improve recovery; antivirals sometimes used | Knowing treatment helps coordinate care and set expectations |
                           | Bilateral Vestibulopathy | Ototoxic medications | Gentamicin, furosemide, cisplatin are common causes | Critical to identify — prevents further damage and informs prognosis |

                           ---

                           ### 🔹 9. “Can you walk without support, or do you need to hold onto walls?”

                           | Case | What It Screens For | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |------|---------------------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | Posterior Canal BPPV | Functional mobility | Usually independent; imbalance only during positional changes | If constant imbalance, consider misdiagnosis or comorbidity |
                           | Horizontal Canal BPPV (Geotropic) | Gait stability | Independent ambulator; avoids rolling | Fear of movement may limit function; education reduces kinesiophobia |
                           | Horizontal Canal BPPV (Apogeotropic) | Dynamic balance | May report mild unsteadiness due to persistent nystagmus | Guides need for balance retraining post-treatment |
                           | Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy | Gait ataxia | Often needs support during acute phase | High fall risk; may require cane; guides safety education |
                           | Labyrinthitis | Severe imbalance | Requires assistance with ambulation initially | Fall risk is high; safety planning essential |
                           | Bilateral Vestibulopathy | Chronic gait instability | Often uses cane or wall support, especially in dark | This is a major functional limitation; guides assistive device prescription |

                           ---

                           ### 🔹 10. “Do you live alone or with someone who can help you?”

                           | Case | What It Screens For | Why We Ask It | Why We Don’t Skip It |
                           |------|---------------------|---------------|-----------------------|
                           | All Cases | Safety and support system | Assesses fall risk and ability to respond to acute episodes | Living alone increases risk during vertigo attacks; may require home modifications or temporary support |
                           | BPPV (All Types) | Risk during positional changes | Falls can occur when rolling in bed | Safety education is critical; recommend side-lying technique |
                           | Acute Unilateral Vestibulopathy | Supervision during acute phase | Patient may be unable to ambulate safely | May need temporary assistance; affects discharge planning |
                           | Labyrinthitis | Support during hearing + balance loss | Dual sensory loss increases disorientation | Higher risk of injury; may require caregiver involvement |
                           | Bilateral Vestibulopathy | Long-term safety | Chronic imbalance increases fall risk, especially at night | May need night lights, grab bars, or assistive device for independence |

                           ---

                           This structured, question-first approach ensures that each clinical inquiry is used strategically across diagnoses, promoting efficient, accurate, and patient-centered evaluation. By understanding how the same question yields different insights depending on the underlying pathology, you can streamline your exam, prioritize key tests, and avoid misdiagnosis.
